newsitem.title: USA: Details of prospective balanced budget accord.
newsitem.headline: Details of prospective balanced budget accord.

text.p: The White House and Republican and Democratic lawmakers moved within sight of a plan to balance the budget by 2002 and provide tax cuts for millions of Americans.
With many provisions still being negotiated, lawmakers outlined the following tentative details of the prospective agreement.

The plan includes an overall tax cut of about $135 billion spread over five years. This tax cut would be partially paid for with $50 billion in other taxes. While not specified in the budget, congressional sources said it was assumed the airline ticket tax would raise $35 billion and that user fees and other higher taxes would make up the remainder.

This net tax cut of $85 billion would include a child care tax credit which some lawmakers said would be set at $500 per child, a broad-based capital gains tax cut, relief from estate taxes paid on inheritances worth more than $600,000, and a tax break to help pay for higher education.

The specific tax rates would be set later by the House Ways and Means Committee and the Senate Finance Committee whose chairmen have strongly resisted efforts by the White House to dictate tax specifics as part of the budget.
Still unresolved was whether the tax plan would include the president's proposed tax credit for clean up of toxic waste in urban areas.

A major part of the savings required to bring down the deficit would be found in the Medicare health care programme for the elderly which would see a $115 billion reduction over five years. The bulk of the savings would come from scaling back payments to doctors, hospitals, managed care plans and other health providers.

Talks were continuing on proposals that would force beneficiaries to pay higher premiums under the optional Medicare Part B programme that covers doctors' care. Medicare recipients now pay $43.80 per month, 25 percent of the Part B premium.

The higher premium might be used to cover home health care services that the White House wants to shift from the hospital trust fund into Part B. The poor would be given an exemption from the higher rate. Republicans and the White House had also been talking about forcing more affluent seniors to pay higher Medicare Part B premiums.

The plan includes gross cuts of about $25 billion over five years in the Medicaid programme for the poor, elderly and disabled. It would set a per person federal spending cap on the programme, which is now an open-ended entitlement, jointly funded by the states and Washington. The proposal also calls for cuts in Medicaid payments to hospitals that serve a large number of poor people.

The National Governors Association adamantly opposes the per person cap, calling it a cost shift to the states and warning it will them to cut poor women and children off the rolls if programme costs grow faster than expected.
Sen. Frank Lautenberg of New Jersey, senior Democrat on the Senate Budget Committee, said the plan would cut federal spending on general government domestic programmes by $68 billion over five years.
Defence spending would be cut $80 billion from the current estimate of spending increases over the five years.
In addition, President Clinton would receive $32 billion for his education, environment and other new initiatives.
The administration won inclusion of a new child health programme to provide health care coverage for five million children now without insurance.

Legal immigrants who were in the country before Aug 22, 1996 when a new welfare law went into effect would continue to be eligible for federal disability aid, at a cost of about $10 billion. Under the welfare law, hundreds of thousands of legal immigrants will lose disability benefits this summer.
